source.title: Unveiling Memorization-Generalization Coexistence: A Case Study on Arithmetic Tasks with Label Noise

page_placements.theme: Latent generalizing subnetworks and structural search

record.tranche_reason: It studies delayed generalization on modular arithmetic, but with two-layer networks trained under label noise rather than reproducing the original training setup.
record.gate_note: The paper's own modular-arithmetic learning dynamics and frequency-filtration outcomes are recorded below. Cited findings from other work are not rows. The MNIST results concern the early ordering of clean- and noisy-label fitting, not delayed generalization.
record.test_reason: It reports its own delayed test-accuracy rise after training accuracy saturates on modular arithmetic, in a new setting with label-noise corruption. It also varies weight decay across optimizers and reports how fast grokking happens. That is a new setting with results on V1 and V5, not a replication of the original recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors also conclude that model-wise double descent holds under label noise, so bigger models generalize better in the over-parameterized regime given suitable optimization and regularization. They also find noisy labels are memorized faster than clean labels early in full-batch training. Grokking under noise is a supporting appendix observation, not a headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses two-layer networks on modular arithmetic with explicit label corruption, varied widths, optimizers, and weight decay; the Transformer experiment is also on synthetic arithmetic. This is not the original study's training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports grokking-speed differences with noise ratio and weight decay: lower noise ratios grok faster; larger weight decay generally speeds grokking for AdamW and Muon, but the trend is not evident for Adam. Results also vary with optimizer, activation, architecture, and model width.

fits_no_version.finding: Frequency filtration of trained networks recovers near-perfect test accuracy under 80% label noise, and raises Transformer test accuracy from 76.8% to 87.8%. A generalizing Fourier structure coexists with noise memorization at the end of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under label noise, networks contain a latent generalizing Fourier circuit masked by memorization, which post-hoc filtering can extract.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower label-noise ratios grok faster across all optimizers. Noisy labels are memorized faster than clean ones early in full-batch training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-noise ratio modulates grokking speed and early fitting order.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results are reported in the text. Much of the learning-dynamics evidence is in figures, and the tested tasks are controlled arithmetic tasks rather than realistic data. Raw near-perfect test accuracy after delayed generalization is not established for all noisy settings.
record.rows_left_out: The many separate width × noise-ratio × weight-decay curves in Figures 19–21 and the broader frequency-filtration sweeps in Figures 5 and 23–25 are not enumerated individually; the text's aggregate findings and the explicitly tabulated Transformer comparison are retained. End-of-training double-descent curves are omitted because they do not measure the delayed-generalization timing in V1.

untested.parts: Two parts are untested: a jump from chance to near-perfect raw test accuracy, and the delay growing as the training set shrinks. Training ratio is varied only for end-of-training results.

Everything is untested. There is no tracking of circuit formation over training, no cleanup of memorizing components, and no progress measures. The Fourier structure is analysed only at end of training.
Everything is untested. There are no grokking delays on non-algorithmic data and no manipulation of initialization scale. The MNIST result concerns early noisy-versus-clean fitting order only.
Everything is untested. The Transformer is trained only on synthetic modular addition.
Untested: efficiency of the generalizing versus memorizing circuit, a critical dataset size, and ungrokking.
Untested: whether different runs or architectures converge to the same or different algorithms. Phase alignment with the analytic solution is shown, but no alternative algorithms are compared.
Everything is untested. There is no test of optimizer-instability or floating-point artifacts.

missing.versions: none (bears on fits_no_version; relevant context for V1 under noise)

missing.what: SGD dynamics: test accuracy still low and rising at 200,000 epochs, with generalization in only one hyperparameter setting
missing.versions: V1 (scope: optimizer dependence of delayed generalization)

record.verdict_notes: Grokking is secondary in this paper: the learning-curve evidence is in appendix figures, with text-only aggregate claims and no seeds or uncertainty. The weight-decay rows bear on V5 only weakly; they show speed, not the efficiency mechanism. Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because the label-noise setting is new rather than a different method on the original question.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports delayed test improvement after training accuracy reaches 100%, but does not establish that raw test accuracy reaches near-perfect levels in each setting or that the delay grows as the training set shrinks. It varies training ratios for end-of-training results, not for the reported long-timescale dynamics.

The paper analyzes an end-state frequency structure and extracts it post-training; it does not track gradual circuit formation, later removal of memorizing components during training, or whether continuous progress measures anticipate the test-accuracy jump.

It does not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data or switch the delay through initialization scale or weight norm. The MNIST experiment reports early clean/noisy fitting, not delayed generalization.
The Transformer experiment uses synthetic modular addition, not realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
It varies weight decay and reports grokking speed, but does not measure whether lower norm selects a more efficient circuit, establish a critical dataset size, or report ungrokking below that size.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for the delay.
